concepts.name: Square identities
concepts.description: (a + b)² and (a − b)² expand to a² ± 2ab + b², replacing a slow expansion with a direct formula.

concepts.name: Difference of squares
concepts.description: a² − b² factorises instantly as (a + b)(a − b), turning subtraction of two squares into one product.

concepts.name: Cube identities
concepts.description: (a + b)³ and (a − b)³ expand to four terms each, useful for cubes of sums and differences.

concepts.name: Sum and difference of cubes
concepts.description: a³ + b³ and a³ − b³ each factorise into a linear factor times a quadratic factor.

concepts.name: Applying identities numerically
concepts.description: Rewriting a number as a sum or difference near a round number lets an identity replace heavy arithmetic.

concepts.name: x + 1/x and its powers
concepts.description: From x + 1/x = k alone: x² + 1/x² = k² − 2, x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k, and every higher power by squaring or multiplying earlier ones. With x − 1/x the cross terms change sign, and (x + 1/x)² − (x − 1/x)² = 4. x² − kx + 1 = 0 and x = a + √b with a² − b = 1 are the same thing in disguise.

concepts.name: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc
concepts.description: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca) = ½(a + b + c)[(a − b)² + (b − c)² + (c − a)²]. So a + b + c = 0 gives a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc, and a² + b² + c² = ab + bc + ca forces a = b = c.

concepts.name: Least and greatest values from squares
concepts.description: A square is never negative. Rewrite an expression as a square plus a constant, and the constant is its least value: x² + 1/x² = (x − 1/x)² + 2 ≥ 2. A sum of squares is zero only when every square is zero.

formulas.title: Square of a sum or difference
formulas.prompt: What do (a + b)² and (a − b)² expand to?
formulas.formula:
(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²
formulas.explanation: The middle term 2ab is easy to forget; only its sign changes between the two identities.

formulas.title: Difference of squares
formulas.explanation: This turns a subtraction of two squares into a single product, which is often much easier to compute or factorise further.
formulas.commonMistake: Writing a² − b² as (a − b)², which loses the cross term.

formulas.title: Cube of a sum or difference
formulas.prompt: What do (a + b)³ and (a − b)³ expand to?
formulas.formula:
(a + b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³
(a − b)³ = a³ − 3a²b + 3ab² − b³
formulas.explanation: The signs alternate in the difference version; the coefficients 1, 3, 3, 1 stay the same in both.
formulas.commonMistake: Using only two terms, as if cubing worked like squaring.

formulas.title: Sum and difference of cubes
formulas.prompt: How do a³ + b³ and a³ − b³ factorise?
formulas.formula:
a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²)
a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²)
formulas.explanation: The linear factor matches the sign of the original expression; the quadratic factor always has the opposite sign in its middle term.
formulas.commonMistake: Getting the sign of the middle term ab wrong in the quadratic factor.

formulas.title: Using identities on numbers
formulas.prompt: How do identities speed up arithmetic like 105² or 97 × 103?
formulas.formula: Write the number as (round number ± small amount), then apply the matching identity
formulas.explanation: Once the number is split this way, the identity replaces long multiplication with a couple of small computations.
formulas.commonMistake: Splitting the number incorrectly, or forgetting the middle term.

formulas.title: When a + b + c = 0
formulas.prompt: a + b + c = 0. What is a³ + b³ + c³?
formulas.formula: If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc
formulas.explanation: It comes from a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca), whose first factor is zero.
formulas.commonMistake: Using it when the sum is not zero.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find (x − y)³ + (y − z)³ + (z − x)³ in factored form.

formulas.title: x + 1/x given
formulas.prompt: You know x + 1/x = k. What are x² + 1/x² and x³ + 1/x³?
formulas.explanation: Square or cube x + 1/x; the cross terms are constants because x × 1/x = 1.
formulas.commonMistake: Writing x² + 1/x² = k², forgetting the 2 from the middle term.
formulas.applicationPrompt: If x − 1/x = 4, find x² + 1/x² (hint: the sign of the middle term changes).

formulas.title: The x + 1/x ladder
formulas.prompt: x + 1/x = k. How do you get x⁴ + 1/x⁴, x⁵ + 1/x⁵ and x⁶ + 1/x⁶ without finding x?
formulas.formula:
x² + 1/x² = k² − 2
x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k
x⁴ + 1/x⁴ = (x² + 1/x²)² − 2
x⁵ + 1/x⁵ = (x² + 1/x²)(x³ + 1/x³) − k
x⁶ + 1/x⁶ = (x³ + 1/x³)² − 2
formulas.explanation: Squaring xⁿ + 1/xⁿ gives x²ⁿ + 1/x²ⁿ plus a middle term 2, because xⁿ × 1/xⁿ = 1. Multiplying (x² + 1/x²)(x³ + 1/x³) gives x⁵ + 1/x⁵ plus the cross terms x + 1/x. So each rung comes from earlier rungs, and all of them from k.
formulas.commonMistake: Writing x⁴ + 1/x⁴ = k⁴ − 2. Square the rung below, (k² − 2)², not k itself.

formulas.title: x − 1/x and x + 1/x together
formulas.prompt: You know x − 1/x = m. What are x² + 1/x², x³ − 1/x³ and x + 1/x?
formulas.explanation: Squaring x − 1/x gives x² − 2 + 1/x², so the 2 is added back. Cubing gives x³ − 1/x³ − 3(x − 1/x), so 3m is added back. The two squares differ by 4 because (x + 1/x)² − (x − 1/x)² = 4 × x × 1/x.
formulas.commonMistake: Using k² − 2 and k³ − 3k here. With a minus sign the cross terms come back with a plus: m² + 2 and m³ + 3m.

formulas.title: x + 1/x in disguise
formulas.prompt: How do x² − kx + 1 = 0, and x = a + √b with a² − b = 1, turn into "x + 1/x = …"?
formulas.formula:
x² − kx + 1 = 0  ⇒  divide by x  ⇒  x + 1/x = k
x = a + √b with a² − b = 1  ⇒  1/x = a − √b  ⇒  x + 1/x = 2a
Given x² + 1/x² = N: x + 1/x = √(N + 2), x − 1/x = √(N − 2) (for x > 1)
formulas.explanation: Dividing x² − kx + 1 = 0 by x leaves x − k + 1/x = 0. And (a + √b)(a − √b) = a² − b = 1, so a − √b is exactly 1/x. Going back from x² + 1/x² = N, add or take away the 2 and take the square root.
formulas.commonMistake: Assuming 1/(a + √b) = a − √b without checking that a² − b = 1. For x = 3 + √5, the product is 4, so 1/x = (3 − √5)/4.

formulas.title: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc
formulas.prompt: How does a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc factorise, and how do you find it from a + b + c and ab + bc + ca?
formulas.formula:
a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca)
= ½(a + b + c)[(a − b)² + (b − c)² + (c − a)²]
a² + b² + c² = (a + b + c)² − 2(ab + bc + ca)
formulas.explanation: Multiplying out (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca) leaves only the three cubes and −3abc. The second bracket is half of (a − b)² + (b − c)² + (c − a)², which is how the ½ form arises.
formulas.commonMistake: Taking a² + b² + c² as (a + b + c)² and forgetting to subtract 2(ab + bc + ca).
formulas.applicationPrompt: a + b + c = 6, ab + bc + ca = 11 and abc = 6. Find a³ + b³ + c³.

formulas.title: When a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc
formulas.prompt: When is a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc, and what does a² + b² + c² = ab + bc + ca tell you?
formulas.formula:
a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc  ⇔  a + b + c = 0 or a = b = c
a² + b² + c² = ab + bc + ca  ⇒  a = b = c
(x − y)³ + (y − z)³ + (z − x)³ = 3(x − y)(y − z)(z − x)
formulas.explanation: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc is ½(a + b + c) times a sum of three squares, so it is zero only when the sum is zero or all three squares are zero. The three differences x − y, y − z, z − x always add to 0.
formulas.commonMistake: Concluding a + b + c = 0 from a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc: a = b = c works too.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the value of (x − y)³ + (y − z)³ + (z − x)³ ÷ [(x − y)(y − z)(z − x)].

formulas.title: A square is never negative
formulas.prompt: How do you find the least value of x² + 1/x², 9x² + 1/x² or x² + y² with x + y fixed, without calculus?
formulas.formula:
Rewrite as (a square) + constant: the least value is the constant, reached when the square is 0
x² + 1/x² = (x − 1/x)² + 2 ≥ 2
x² + y² = ½[(x + y)² + (x − y)²],  xy = ¼[(x + y)² − (x − y)²]
A sum of squares = 0  ⇒  each square = 0
formulas.explanation: No real square is below 0, so a square plus c is never below c, and equals c only where the square vanishes. With x + y fixed, the only part that changes is (x − y)², so x = y gives the least x² + y² and the largest xy.
formulas.example: 9x² + 1/x² = (3x − 1/x)² + 6, so its least value is 6, at x² = 1/3. And (a − 1)² + (b + 2)² = 0 forces a = 1 and b = −2.
formulas.commonMistake: Adding the least values of separate parts. The parts must reach their least at the same x, so rewrite the whole expression as one square plus a constant.
formulas.applicationPrompt: For real x ≠ 0, find the least value of 4x² + 25/x².

levels.title: Shortcuts for Squares
levels.description: Formulas that replace slow expansion or factorisation with one direct step.

blocks.title: Why identities save time
blocks.body: Expanding (x + 5)² term by term takes a few steps. The identity (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² gives the same answer, x² + 10x + 25, in one line once you know it.

blocks.title: Square identities
blocks.body:
(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²
blocks.caption: Only the sign of the middle term changes between the two.

blocks.body: a² − b² is never (a − b)². The correct factorisation is (a + b)(a − b).

levels.title: Algebraic Identities Formulas
levels.description: Square identities, difference of squares, cube identities, sum/difference of cubes, numeric applications.

levels.title: Direct Expansion and Factorisation
levels.description: Applying the square and difference-of-squares identities directly.

levels.title: Numeric Shortcuts and Rearranging
levels.description: Using identities on numbers, and rearranging them to find hidden quantities.

levels.title: Cubes and Combined Identities
levels.description: Sum and difference of cubes, and identities chained together.

levels.title: Advanced: x + 1/x and Three-Variable Identities
levels.description: Powers of x + 1/x from k alone, x − 1/x, a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc, and least values from squares.

blocks.title: One number, a whole ladder
blocks.body: When a question gives x + 1/x = k, never solve for x. Squaring gives (x + 1/x)² = x² + 2 + 1/x², because the middle term is 2 × x × 1/x = 2. Cubing gives (x + 1/x)³ = x³ + 1/x³ + 3(x + 1/x). So x² + 1/x² and x³ + 1/x³ need only k, and every higher power follows from them.

blocks.title: The ladder
blocks.body:
x² + 1/x² = k² − 2
x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k
x⁴ + 1/x⁴ = (x² + 1/x²)² − 2
x⁵ + 1/x⁵ = (x² + 1/x²)(x³ + 1/x³) − k
x⁶ + 1/x⁶ = (x³ + 1/x³)² − 2
blocks.caption: Squaring a rung doubles the power: take 2 away. Multiplying two neighbouring rungs adds the powers: take k away.

blocks.title: x + 1/x = 3
blocks.body: x² + 1/x² = 9 − 2 = 7. x³ + 1/x³ = 27 − 9 = 18. x⁴ + 1/x⁴ = 7² − 2 = 47. x⁵ + 1/x⁵ = 7 × 18 − 3 = 123. x⁶ + 1/x⁶ = 18² − 2 = 322. We never needed x itself, which is (3 + √5)/2.

blocks.title: x − 1/x, and going back
blocks.body: With x − 1/x = m the cross terms change sign: x² + 1/x² = m² + 2 and x³ − 1/x³ = m³ + 3m. The two are tied together: (x + 1/x)² − (x − 1/x)² = 4, and x² − 1/x² = (x + 1/x)(x − 1/x). Given x² + 1/x² = N, go back with x + 1/x = √(N + 2) and x − 1/x = √(N − 2), choosing the sign from what you know about x.

blocks.title: With a minus sign
blocks.caption: m = x − 1/x can be any real number; x + 1/x cannot lie between −2 and 2.

blocks.body: Spot the disguises. x² − 5x + 1 = 0 divided by x is x + 1/x = 5. x = 2 + √3 has 1/x = 2 − √3, because (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1, so x + 1/x = 4.

blocks.title: Three variables: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc
blocks.body: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc factorises as (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca). The second bracket is half of (a − b)² + (b − c)² + (c − a)², a sum of squares. Two results follow. If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc. And the expression is 0 only when a + b + c = 0 or a = b = c.

blocks.title: The three-variable identity
blocks.body:
a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca)
= ½(a + b + c)[(a − b)² + (b − c)² + (c − a)²]
a² + b² + c² = (a + b + c)² − 2(ab + bc + ca)
blocks.caption: Given a + b + c and ab + bc + ca, find a² + b² + c² first.

blocks.title: Bases that add to zero
blocks.body: 25³ − 15³ − 10³ is a³ + b³ + c³ with a = 25, b = −15, c = −10, which add to 0. So it equals 3 × 25 × (−15) × (−10) = 11,250. In the same way (x − y)³ + (y − z)³ + (z − x)³ = 3(x − y)(y − z)(z − x), since the three bases always add to 0.

blocks.title: Least values: a square is never negative
blocks.body: x² + 1/x² = (x − 1/x)² + 2, so it is never below 2 and equals 2 at x = ±1. In general, rewrite an expression as a square plus a constant; the constant is the least value. With x + y fixed, x² + y² = ½[(x + y)² + (x − y)²] is least and xy = ¼[(x + y)² − (x − y)²] is greatest when x = y. And a sum of squares equal to 0 forces every square to be 0, which is why a² + b² + c² = ab + bc + ca makes a = b = c.
The least value of a sum is not the sum of the least values unless both happen at the same x. Rewrite the whole expression as one square plus a constant before reading off the answer.

levels.title: Practice: x + 1/x and Three-Variable Identities
levels.description: Higher powers, x − 1/x, sums of cubes whose bases add to zero, and completing squares.

levels.title: Challenge: Advanced Identities
levels.description: Disguised x + 1/x, surds, going back down the ladder, a³ + b³ + c³ and least values.

questions.question: What is (x + 5)² expanded?
questions.explanation: Using (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² with a = x, b = 5: x² + 10x + 25.
questions.method: Apply the identity term by term.

hints.text: Do not forget the middle term 2ab.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the middle term, giving x² + 25.

questions.question: What is (x − 7)² expanded?
questions.explanation: Using (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² with a = x, b = 7: x² − 14x + 49.
questions.method: The middle term is negative here.

hints.text: The sign of the middle term matches the sign inside the bracket.

commonMistakes: Using a plus sign for the middle term.

questions.question: What is x² − 64 factorised?
questions.method: Recognise the perfect square.

hints.text: 64 is a perfect square.

commonMistakes: Writing (x − 8)², which is wrong.

questions.question: The expansion of (a − b)² differs from (a + b)² only in the sign of
questions.explanation: Both expansions have the same a² and b² terms; only the middle term 2ab changes sign.
questions.method: Compare the two identities term by term.

hints.text: a² and b² are always positive.

commonMistakes: Assuming the whole expansion flips sign.

questions.question: Using an identity, what is 105²?
questions.method: Split 105 as 100 + 5, then apply (a+b)².

hints.text: Split the number into a round part and a small part.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the middle term 1,000.

questions.question: If a + b = 12 and ab = 27, what is a² + b²?
questions.explanation: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², so a² + b² = (a+b)² − 2ab = 144 − 54 = 90.
questions.method: Rearrange the square identity to isolate a² + b².

hints.text: (a+b)² already contains a² + b² and 2ab together.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract 2ab, not just ab.

questions.question: If a − b = 5 and a² + b² = 53, what is ab?
questions.explanation: (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², so 25 = 53 − 2ab, giving 2ab = 28 and ab = 14.
questions.method: Use the difference-square identity to isolate ab.

hints.text: Substitute the known values into (a−b)² = a² − 2ab + b².

commonMistakes: Sign error when isolating 2ab.

questions.question: If a = 7 and b = 3, what is (a + b)² − (a − b)²?
questions.explanation: (a+b)² − (a−b)² = 4ab (the a² and b² terms cancel). So 4 × 7 × 3 = 84.
questions.method: The two square identities differ only in the sign of 2ab.

hints.text: Subtracting the two expansions cancels a² and b².

commonMistakes: Expanding both squares fully instead of using the shortcut.

questions.question: Using the difference of squares, what is 97 × 103?
questions.method: Rewrite as (round − small)(round + small).

hints.text: Both numbers are 3 away from 100.

commonMistakes: Multiplying 97 × 103 directly instead of using the shortcut.

questions.question: What is (2x + 3y)² expanded?
questions.explanation: Using (a+b)² with a = 2x, b = 3y: (2x)² + 2(2x)(3y) + (3y)² = 4x² + 12xy + 9y².
questions.method: Square each term, then double the product for the middle term.

hints.text: Square the coefficients too, not just the variables.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to square the coefficients 2 and 3.

questions.question: If a + b = 8 and a² + b² = 34, what is a³ + b³?
questions.explanation: First find ab: (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b², so 64 = 34 + 2ab, giving ab = 15. Then a³+b³ = (a+b)(a²−ab+b²) = 8(34 − 15) = 8 × 19 = 152.
questions.method: Find ab first, then use the sum-of-cubes identity.

hints.text: You need ab before you can use the cube identity.

commonMistakes: Trying to use the cube identity without first finding ab.

questions.question: What is x³ − 27 factorised?
questions.explanation: 27 = 3³, so x³ − 27 = x³ − 3³ = (x − 3)(x² + 3x + 9), using a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).
questions.method: Identify the cube root, then apply the identity.

hints.text: The middle term of the quadratic factor is +ab, not −ab.

commonMistakes: Using −3x instead of +3x in the quadratic factor.

questions.question: If x + 1/x = 5, what is x² + 1/x²?
questions.explanation: Square both sides: (x + 1/x)² = x² + 2 + 1/x². So 25 = x² + 1/x² + 2, giving x² + 1/x² = 23.
questions.method: Square the given expression, then subtract the constant 2.

hints.text: Squaring (x + 1/x) produces a constant term of 2, not 0.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the +2 that appears when the middle term simplifies.

questions.question: If x + 1/x = 4, what is x³ + 1/x³?
questions.explanation: Cube both sides: (x + 1/x)³ = x³ + 1/x³ + 3 × x × (1/x) × (x + 1/x) = x³ + 1/x³ + 3(x + 1/x). So 64 = x³ + 1/x³ + 3 × 4, and x³ + 1/x³ = 64 − 12 = 52.
questions.method: x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k.

hints.text: Do not solve for x: cube x + 1/x and see what the extra terms are.
(a + b)³ = a³ + b³ + 3ab(a + b), and here ab = x × 1/x = 1.
So 4³ = x³ + 1/x³ + 3 × 4.

commonMistakes: Subtracting 3 instead of 3k, which gives 61.
Adding 3k instead of subtracting it, which gives 76.

questions.question: If a + b + c = 9 and ab + bc + ca = 26, what is a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc?
questions.explanation: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca). First a² + b² + c² = 9² − 2 × 26 = 29, so the bracket is 29 − 26 = 3 and the value is 9 × 3 = 27. (a, b, c = 2, 3, 4 fit: 8 + 27 + 64 − 72 = 27.)
solutionSteps: a² + b² + c² = (a + b + c)² − 2(ab + bc + ca) = 81 − 52 = 29.
a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca = 29 − 26 = 3.
questions.method: Factorise as (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca), finding a² + b² + c² first.

hints.text: Which identity has a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc on one side?
It is (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca); you still need a² + b² + c².
a² + b² + c² = 9² − 2 × 26.

commonMistakes: Stopping at 9 × 29 = 261, without subtracting ab + bc + ca from a² + b² + c².
Taking a² + b² + c² as 9² = 81 (giving 9 × 55 = 495), or cubing the sum alone (729).

questions.question: For real x ≠ 0, what is the least value of 9x² + 1/x²?
questions.explanation: (3x − 1/x)² = 9x² − 6 + 1/x², so 9x² + 1/x² = (3x − 1/x)² + 6. A square is never negative, so the expression is never below 6, and it equals 6 when 3x = 1/x, that is x² = 1/3.
solutionSteps: Pick the square whose cross term is a constant: (3x − 1/x)² = 9x² − 6 + 1/x².
It equals 6 at x² = 1/3, so the least value is 6.
questions.method: Write the expression as a square plus a constant.

hints.text: Which square has 9x² and 1/x² as its outer terms?
Its middle term is the constant −6, so 9x² + 1/x² = (3x − 1/x)² + 6.

commonMistakes: Copying "x² + 1/x² ≥ 2" without the coefficient 9, or taking the middle term as 3 and forgetting its factor 2.
Putting x = 1, which gives 10, not the least value.

questions.question: If x + 1/x = 3, what is x⁴ + 1/x⁴?
questions.explanation: Climb the ladder: x² + 1/x² = 3² − 2 = 7. Squaring again, (x² + 1/x²)² = x⁴ + 2 + 1/x⁴, so x⁴ + 1/x⁴ = 7² − 2 = 47. Each squaring creates a middle term 2 that must be taken away.
questions.method: Square twice, subtracting 2 each time.

hints.text: Get to the fourth power in two squarings, not one.
First x² + 1/x² = k² − 2.
Then square x² + 1/x² = 7 and take 2 away again.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the second −2, which gives 49.
Squaring only once: k⁴ − 2 = 79, or k⁴ = 81.

questions.question: If x > 0 and x − 1/x = 4, what is x + 1/x?
questions.explanation: (x + 1/x)² and (x − 1/x)² have the same x² + 1/x² but middle terms +2 and −2, so they differ by 4: (x + 1/x)² = (x − 1/x)² + 4 = 16 + 4 = 20. As x > 0, x + 1/x is positive, so it is √20 = 2√5. (Here x = 2 + √5.)

hints.text: Both expressions square to x² + 1/x² plus or minus something.

commonMistakes: Subtracting 4 instead of adding it: √12 = 2√3.
Adding 2 as for x² + 1/x²: √18 = 3√2 (or 4 + 2 = 6 without squaring).

questions.question: x − 1/x = 3. Match each expression with its value.
questions.explanation: Squaring x − 1/x gives x² − 2 + 1/x², so x² + 1/x² = 9 + 2 = 11. (x + 1/x)² = (x − 1/x)² + 4 = 13. Cubing gives x³ − 1/x³ − 3(x − 1/x), so x³ − 1/x³ = 27 + 9 = 36. Squaring x² + 1/x² = 11 gives x⁴ + 1/x⁴ = 121 − 2 = 119.
questions.method: With x − 1/x the cross terms come back with a plus sign; from x² + 1/x² on, square as usual.

hints.text: Square and cube x − 1/x; the cross terms are constants or multiples of x − 1/x.
x² + 1/x² = m² + 2 and x³ − 1/x³ = m³ + 3m.
For x⁴ + 1/x⁴, square x² + 1/x² = 11 and take 2 away.

commonMistakes: Using the plus-sign rules: 3² − 2 = 7 and 3³ − 9 = 18.
Squaring 11 for x⁴ + 1/x⁴ without taking 2 away (121).

questions.question: Without cubing each number, find the value of 25³ − 15³ − 10³.
questions.method: If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc.

hints.text: Treat the minus signs as part of the numbers: 25, −15 and −10.
What do 25, −15 and −10 add up to?
Their sum is 0, so the sum of cubes is 3 × their product.

commonMistakes: Dropping the 3 and giving 25 × 15 × 10 = 3,750.
Getting a negative answer by losing one of the two minus signs.

questions.question: For distinct x, y, z, what is the value of [(x − y)³ + (y − z)³ + (z − x)³] ÷ [9(x − y)(y − z)(z − x)]?
questions.explanation: The three bases x − y, y − z and z − x add up to 0, so the sum of their cubes is 3 times their product: 3(x − y)(y − z)(z − x). Dividing by 9(x − y)(y − z)(z − x) leaves 3/9 = 1/3. (Try x, y, z = 5, 3, 2: (8 + 1 − 27) ÷ (9 × 2 × 1 × (−3)) = −18 ÷ −54 = 1/3.)
solutionSteps: So the numerator is 3(x − y)(y − z)(z − x).
questions.method: Three bases that add to 0: the sum of cubes is 3 × the product.

hints.text: Add the three bases x − y, y − z and z − x.
They add to 0, so use a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc.
The numerator is 3(x − y)(y − z)(z − x); now divide.

commonMistakes: Thinking the cubes cancel because the bases add to 0, giving 0.
Dropping the 9 in the denominator (3) or the 3 in 3abc (1/9).

questions.question: Real numbers a, b, c satisfy a² + b² + c² + 14 = 2(a − 2b + 3c). What is a + b + c?
questions.explanation: Bring everything to one side and complete three squares: a² − 2a + 1 + b² + 4b + 4 + c² − 6c + 9 = 0, since 1 + 4 + 9 = 14. That is (a − 1)² + (b + 2)² + (c − 3)² = 0. Squares are never negative, so each is 0: a = 1, b = −2, c = 3, and a + b + c = 2.
solutionSteps: Each square is 0: a = 1, b = −2, c = 3.
questions.method: Complete the squares; a sum of squares is 0 only if each is 0.

hints.text: Move everything to the left-hand side and look for perfect squares.
The constant 14 splits as 1 + 4 + 9 to complete (a − 1)², (b + 2)² and (c − 3)².
A sum of squares equal to 0 makes every square 0.

commonMistakes: Reading b = 2 from (b + 2)², which gives 6.
Flipping every sign (a = −1, b = 2, c = −3), which gives −2.

questions.question: If x² − 3x + 1 = 0, what is x⁶ + 1/x⁶?
questions.explanation: x is not 0, so divide the equation by x: x − 3 + 1/x = 0, that is x + 1/x = 3. Then x³ + 1/x³ = 27 − 9 = 18, and squaring, x⁶ + 1/x⁶ = 18² − 2 = 322. (Or x² + 1/x² = 7 and x⁶ + 1/x⁶ = 7³ − 3 × 7 = 322.)
questions.method: Divide by x to get x + 1/x, then square the cube rung.

hints.text: An equation x² − kx + 1 = 0 is x + 1/x = k in disguise.
Divide by x: x + 1/x = 3. Which rung, squared, gives the sixth power?
x³ + 1/x³ = 18; square it and take 2 away.

commonMistakes: Squaring 18 without taking 2 away (324).
Cubing 3 twice as if x⁶ + 1/x⁶ were k⁶ (729).

questions.question: If x = 5 + 2√6, what is x³ + 1/x³?
questions.explanation: (5 + 2√6)(5 − 2√6) = 25 − 24 = 1, so 1/x = 5 − 2√6 and x + 1/x = 10. Then x³ + 1/x³ = 10³ − 3 × 10 = 970. (Numerically x ≈ 9.899 and x³ ≈ 969.999, with 1/x³ making up the rest.)
questions.method: Find 1/x by the conjugate, add to get k, then use k³ − 3k.

hints.text: Multiply 5 + 2√6 by 5 − 2√6. What do you get?
The product is 1, so 1/x = 5 − 2√6 and x + 1/x = 10.
Now x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k with k = 10.

commonMistakes: Giving k³ = 1000 and forgetting −3k.
Subtracting 3 instead of 3k (997), or adding 3k instead of subtracting it (1030).

questions.question: If x > 0 and x² + 1/x² = 34, what is x³ + 1/x³?
questions.explanation: Go back down the ladder first: (x + 1/x)² = x² + 1/x² + 2 = 36, and x > 0 makes x + 1/x positive, so x + 1/x = 6. Then x³ + 1/x³ = 6³ − 3 × 6 = 216 − 18 = 198. (Here x = 3 + 2√2.)
questions.method: Recover x + 1/x = √(N + 2), then cube.

hints.text: Find x + 1/x first; you cannot cube x² + 1/x² directly.
x + 1/x = √36 = 6; now use k³ − 3k.

commonMistakes: Giving 6³ = 216 and forgetting −3k.
Adding 3k instead of subtracting it (234), or subtracting 3 instead of 3k (213).

questions.question: If a + b + c = 6, a² + b² + c² = 14 and abc = 6, what is a³ + b³ + c³?
questions.explanation: First ab + bc + ca = (6² − 14) ÷ 2 = 11. Then a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca) = 6 × (14 − 11) = 18, so a³ + b³ + c³ = 18 + 3 × 6 = 36. (a, b, c = 1, 2, 3 fit: 1 + 8 + 27 = 36.)
questions.method: Find ab + bc + ca, use the identity, then add 3abc back.

hints.text: The identity gives a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc; you will need ab + bc + ca for it.
2(ab + bc + ca) = (a + b + c)² − (a² + b² + c²).
Work out 6 × (14 − 11), then add 3abc back.

commonMistakes: Stopping at a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = 18, or adding back abc instead of 3abc (24).
Multiplying the sum by the sum of squares, 6 × 14 = 84.

questions.question: If a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc for real numbers a, b, c, then a + b + c must be 0.
questions.explanation: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = ½(a + b + c)[(a − b)² + (b − c)² + (c − a)²]. It is 0 when a + b + c = 0 or when the bracket is 0, which happens when a = b = c. For example a = b = c = 1: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 = 3abc, yet a + b + c = 3. So the statement is false.
solutionSteps: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = ½(a + b + c)[(a − b)² + (b − c)² + (c − a)²].
The product is 0 if either factor is 0.
a = b = c = 1 gives 3 = 3 with a + b + c = 3, so the statement is false.
questions.method: Factorise and ask when each factor can be 0; test a = b = c.

hints.text: Write a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc as a product of two factors.
The second factor is half a sum of the squares of differences. When is that 0?
Try a = b = c = 1.

commonMistakes: Reading the shortcut "a + b + c = 0 ⇒ a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc" backwards.

questions.question: For real x ≠ 0, what is the least value of x² + 1/x² − 2(x − 1/x)?
questions.explanation: Let m = x − 1/x, which can be any real number. Then x² + 1/x² = m² + 2, so the expression is m² − 2m + 2 = (m − 1)² + 1. Its least value is 1, reached when x − 1/x = 1 (x = (1 + √5)/2 works). Putting x = 1 gives 2, but that is not where the minimum is.
solutionSteps: Put m = x − 1/x; then x² + 1/x² = m² + 2.
questions.method: Rewrite in terms of x − 1/x, then complete the square.

hints.text: Write everything in terms of one quantity, m = x − 1/x.
Complete the square in m² − 2m + 2.

commonMistakes: Putting x = 1, where x² + 1/x² is least, which gives 2.
Writing x² + 1/x² as m² (giving −1) or as m² − 2 (giving −3) instead of m² + 2.
